analysis.one_liner: Requires federal judges to report stock trades within 45 days and puts their financial disclosures online.
analysis.headline: The bill passed both chambers by voice vote and was signed into law on May 13, 2022 as Public Law 117-125.
analysis.plain_summary: This law requires federal judges, bankruptcy judges, and magistrate judges to report stock and other securities trades over $1,000 within 45 days, the same standard members of Congress already follow. It also directs the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to post judges' annual financial disclosure reports on a free, searchable public website. The goal is to let litigants and the public see when a judge has money at stake in companies appearing before that judge's court.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who appears in federal court, and the broader public, gains the ability to see a judge's investments and recent trades. Parties in a case can check whether the judge holds stock in a company involved in the litigation, and journalists and watchdog groups get a searchable database of judges' finances instead of paper records available only on request. Members of Congress already file periodic transaction reports; this law puts federal judges under the same rule [S2][S5][S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court litigants, journalists, and the public

how_it_helps.text: Federal judges, bankruptcy judges, and magistrate judges must file a report within 45 days of any purchase, sale, or exchange of stocks, bonds, commodities futures, or other securities worth more than $1,000 — the same periodic reporting standard that applies to members of Congress.

The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts must build a free online database and post each judge's financial disclosure report within 90 days of the filing deadline, in a full-text searchable, sortable, and downloadable format that anyone can use.

The online publication requirement took effect on a fixed timetable: the database was due within 180 days of enactment and the trading-disclosure rule applied to transactions starting 90 days after the law was signed, so judges' stock activity became visible to the public rather than discoverable only through laborious records requests.

The law was tailored to protect judges and their families: reports can be redacted or withheld from immediate publication if the Judicial Conference finds that revealing personal information could endanger a judge or a family member.

analysis.who_pays: Federal judges, bankruptcy judges, and magistrate judges bear the main cost: they lose the ability to trade stocks quietly and must file regular reports disclosing their finances. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts pays the administrative cost of building and maintaining the public database. The law imposes no cost on private businesses or taxpayers beyond the courts' administrative budget [S2][S6].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal judges and the courts' administrative office

drawbacks.text: The law requires disclosure but does not prohibit anything: judges remain free to buy and sell individual stocks, including in companies with cases before them, and the only check on a conflict is a recusal request by the parties. Reformers who wanted a ban on judicial stock trading did not get one in this law.

The safety exception is broad enough that a report can be withheld from immediate publication if the Judicial Conference, a body made up of sitting judges, finds that disclosure could endanger a judge or family member — so the judiciary itself controls the main carve-out from the transparency requirement.

The database requirement includes an escape valve: the Administrative Office can notify Congress in writing that it needs more time, delaying the searchable database beyond the 180-day deadline, as long as reports remain available by other means.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in scope: it exposes judges' financial conflicts rather than eliminating them, and a judge determined to trade around a conflict can still do so, at the price of visible disclosure. The cost is small — some loss of financial privacy for judges, an administrative burden on the courts, and a self-administered safety exception — and it is weighed against giving every litigant and reporter the same window into judicial finances that the public has long had into Congress's. This is a genuine transparency win, though only a first step compared with divestment requirements.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by voice vote and the President signed it on May 13, 2022.

narrative.text: Senator John Cornyn introduced the bill in October 2021 with bipartisan support — 4 Democratic and 3 Republican senators signed on as cosponsors.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee never marked it up; instead the full Senate discharged the committee by unanimous consent on February 17, 2022, and passed the bill without amendment by voice vote the same day.

The House took it up on April 27, 2022 under a suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure that limits debate and blocks amendments — and passed it by voice vote, with Representative Hakeem Jeffries moving to suspend the rules and pass the bill.

The President signed it on May 13, 2022, making it Public Law 117-125; the underlying requirement took effect for transactions occurring 90 days after enactment, with the public database due within 180 days.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead: litigants, journalists, and watchdog groups gained a searchable window into the finances of the federal judges who decide their cases. Stock-holding judges are the ones who gave something up — quiet trading is now visible — though the law left their right to trade intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; judges' stock trading now visible

for.name: Wall Street Journal investigative reporting
for.what_they_did: Published a 2021 investigation documenting federal judges hearing cases involving companies in which they owned stock, fueling public and congressional pressure for the bill.

against.name: Judicial Conference / Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts
against.role: Governing body and administrative arm of the federal judiciary
against.what_they_did: Pressed for years to keep judges' financial disclosures off the internet, citing safety risks to judges; the final law accommodated this by allowing redaction and delayed publication when safety is at issue.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with 4 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors, and both chambers passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Federal judiciary (judges, bankruptcy and magistrate judges)
industries.note: The law strips federal judges of the ability to trade securities without public disclosure and puts their annual financial reports on a free public website. Their interest in keeping finances private runs against the public's interest in knowing when a judge has a stake in a case — though the judiciary's safety exception was written into the law, and trading itself remains legal for judges.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies in federal litigation
industries.note: Companies and their counsel can now check whether the judge hearing their case holds or recently traded their stock, strengthening recusal requests. That cuts both ways for business: it deters judge-shopping advantages from undisclosed conflicts but also exposes more potential recusal pressure in high-stakes cases.
